What does all of this feel like in everyday use? These Mac Minis are more than capable for lots of multitasking and content creation, with the M5 Pro of course having more headroom. I was able to import a batch of 1,253 50-megapixel RAW images (all my recent photos still living on my SD card) from my full-frame Sony camera into Lightroom Classic on the M6 Mac Mini in about 6 minutes and 13 seconds. The same import only went about 30 seconds faster on the M5 Pro Mac Mini. But doing some heavy batch editing with AI subject detection across a selection of 188 photos showed the performance advantage of the M5 Pro. The M6 Mac Mini was decently fast, but even with 24GB of RAM this little torture test hit swap memory and slowed mid-processing. The M5 Pro sailed through and stayed speedier the whole way through. [Image: The M5 Pro model should come in black. If you’re doing video editing, visual effects, or 3D rendering then you’re best served looking at the M5 Pro Mac Mini — or maybe even the Mac Studio if you have the budget. The M6 Mac Mini is more for generalists who do creative work on the side or want an everyday desktop they could use for a very long time, like up to a decade. When I bought a Mac Mini for myself in 2023 I opted for the cheapest M2 Pro. (Yes, I’m plenty jealous of how small the current models are.) It served me well, but these days I’d probably be fine with an M6 Mac Mini. While I often deal with lots of high-res images in Lightroom Classic, photography isn’t my full-time work. If I were editing thousands of photos for hours a day I’d definitely consider the M5 Pro Mac Mini or M5 Max Mac Studio — and then I’d also get my precious SD card slot. And yes, the Mac Minis are great for local AI compute, thanks in part to fast unified memory, and Apple’s leaning into that with the new models. The press release announcing the M6 and M5 Pro chips mentions AI capabilities nearly 40 times. [Image: [Image: Hardware-wise, these Mac Minis are nearly identical to the older ones. They have the same ports as the last-gen model, with two 10Gbps USB-C ports and a headphone jack on the front. On the rear, there are three Thunderbolt ports (TB4 on the M6 model; TB5 on the M5 Pro), plus HDMI 2.1 and an ethernet port. The ethernet has been bumped from 1 gigabit to 2.5Gbps; you can upgrade to 10Gb for $100. Sure, the power button is still on the bottom, but it remains mostly no big deal since the Mini is designed to sip power when idle; you can just put it to sleep instead of turning it off. Apple even added a software feature to somewhat alleviate this by having the Mac Mini turn itself back on after the power is cut. The other thing that’s still the same are the Mac Mini’s crummy little speakers. I’ve owned and used the older, larger M2 Pro Mac Mini for years so I know how you can get by with the built-in speakers when you’re too lazy to put on headphones, but they should only be relied on for hearing the beeps, boops, and “knock brushes” of notifications. There’s now Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support on the 2026 Mac Minis, which is a nice small upgrade. Just like annual phone releases, the new Mac Mini will best serve newcomers and people still running much older models. Do you still have an Intel-based Mac that’s now run out of OS updates with the introduction of macOS 27 Golden Gate? Boy, are you in for a treat. On the software side, I feel the same way about macOS 27 Golden Gate as I did during the developer beta: the visual refinements that tone down Liquid Glass transparency, increase window sidebar legibility, and fix window corner radii are all welcome changes. Golden Gate is an overall nice improvement over macOS 26 Tahoe, even if Siri AI and Apple Intelligence on the Mac are just kinda Fine. [Image: The bottom power button remains weird, but it’s rarely an issue. It could pose a problem if you mount the Mini somewhere hard to reach. Since this year’s upgrade to the Mac Mini is mostly a chip bump, it’s of course a bummer it’s much more expensive. But then again, so is everything else these days. RAMageddon shows no mercy for any manufacturer. Apple’s computers are pricier. Intel and AMD chip costs are rumored to rise soon. Laptops are launching at one price and then changing shortly after. In terms of mini PCs, Minisforum raised its prices and the Framework Desktop is more expensive now than when it launched last year. There are cheaper mini PCs, and there are smaller ones, but none of them truly compete with the Mac Mini’s balance of performance, price, and size — even with the price increase. (Gaming is a different story, of course.) This is our new normal. The Mac Mini is still a great deal; it just doesn’t feel like the steal it used to be. But with the recent price increases hitting MacBook Airs and MacBook Pros, the new Mac Minis remain much cheaper than getting similar chips in a laptop (especially if you already have a monitor, mouse, and keyboard). The base M6 Mac Mini is $400 cheaper than the cheapest M5 MacBook Air, and the base M5 Pro model is $800 less than the MacBook Pro with the same chip and memory. Sadly it doesn’t seem likely we’ll ever see a Mac Mini start at a price like $599 ever again. It’s still an easy recommendation if you want a tiny desktop computer that runs circles around comparably priced PCs and will last for years, but it’ll take time to forget the gut punch that is these price increases. --- M6 / M5 Pro Mac Mini specs (as reviewed) * CPU (M6): Apple M6 (12-core CPU / 12-core GPU) * CPU (M5 Pro): Apple M5 Pro (18-core CPU / 20-core GPU) * Unified memory (M6): 24GB * Unified memory (M5 Pro): 48GB * Storage (M6): 512GB SSD * Storage (M5 Pro): 1TB SSD * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 * Ports (M6): 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 3x Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C (DisplayPort 1.4), 1x HDMI 2.1, RJ45 2.5Gb ethernet, AC power * Ports (M5 Pro): 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 3x Thunderbolt 5 / USB-C (DisplayPort 2.1), 1x HDMI 2.1, RJ45 10Gb ethernet, AC power * Weight (M6): 1.5 pounds / 0.67kg * Weight (M5 Pro): 1.6 pounds / 0.73kg * Dimensions: 5 x 5 x 2 inches / 127 x 127 x 50mm * Price (M6): $1,299 * Price (M5 Pro): $2,899

articles.title: The M5 Ultra Mac Studio tears through our benchmark tests
articles.summary: Apple’s $12,300 Mac Studio with an M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of RAM is outrageously powerful —tilting the scales of our usual benchmark tests.
articles.body: The Mac Studio review unit that Apple sent us to test this year is, put simply, kind of outrageous. It has an M5 Ultra chip with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU, 256GB of RAM, and 4TB of storage and costs $12,299. This thing is not for your typical content creation workloads. It’s for AI developers and some of the most demanding 3D visual effects houses out there. Frankly, our usual benchmarks aren’t cutting it. The latest version of Apple’s most powerful computer begins shipping today with new chips and prices that extend even further into the stratosphere. The new Mac Studio uses the same design that’s been with us since 2022, replete with ultra-fast ports both front and back, now kitted out with either an M5 Max or M5 Ultra chip, compared to the M4 Max or M3 Ultra of last year’s model. [Image: My precious! (I’m talking about the SD card slot, of course.) The M5 Max model starts at a relatively modest $2,499 with an 18-core CPU / 32-core GPU, 36GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. We’ve tested an M5 Max already, in the MacBook Pro, where it starts at $4,099 with the same amount of memory and 2TB of storage (the equivalent Mac Studio costs $3,299). The M5 Ultra is another beast altogether. It starts at $5,499 with 30 CPU cores, 64 GPU cores, 96GB of memory and 1TB of storage. I’ve only had my hands on the new Mac Studio as well as a pair of the latest Mac Minis for a handful of days. That’s enough time to adequately test the M6 and M5 Pro chips in the Mac Mini, and to run our standard benchmarks on the M5 Ultra — but not enough time to seriously challenge it. Conveniently, we still have the similarly specced M3 Ultra Mac Studio from last year — though it was only $8,099 at the time. Aside from CPU core count and architecture, they’re nearly the same, which makes them easy to compare. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is around 30 percent faster than our similarly configured M3 Ultra in both single-core and multicore synthetic CPU tests. It varies more in graphics tests, but some, like the new Geekbench 7 OpenCL test, also saw around a 30 percent uplift. And a heftier GPU rendering test like Cinebench scored 63 percent higher. I’ve never tested anything this fast before. The storage speeds are off the proverbial charts. It renders the classroom test in Blender faster than I can tie my shoes. Our Premiere 4K video export test, which yields an MP4 file of about 1.7GB, is done in about 40 seconds. I can’t get up from my desk and get a cup of coffee that fast without risking a serious burn. [Image: All ports in a storm. Apple is talking a big game about the M5 Ultra being “a monumental step for AI.” I don’t normally run local AI stuff (I just don’t find generative AI and LLM stuff very useful for my work — and I’ve tried). But I want to give it a serious go, so I’m open to suggestions. I’ve already reached out to our great Verge audience for ideas, and I appreciate all of you who commented. (Yes, even those of you with the “Can it run DOOM” jokes. I see you, and it never gets old. I mean, it does. But it doesn’t. I love DOOM.) How long is this going to take me? Hopefully not very long, but it’s going to be a busy couple of months. Google is announcing its whole new line of Googlebook laptops at exactly the same time this article publishes. And there’s a Microsoft event coming up next week that sounds a whole lot like it’ll jumpstart Nvidia’s RTX Spark initiative. There’s never a drought of laptops to test, but this Techtember and Techtober seems like a deluge that’s about to engulf Your Friendly Neighborhood Laptop Reviewer. I know, I know; “So many cool computers to test, what a burden.” Truly, it is a very exciting time for computers. An expensive one, for sure, but I don’t think the space has ever been this dynamic. So I’ll do my best to get back to you when I’ve got something cool to share about the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Feel free to drop more ideas and tips in the comments here. Or email me or DM me on Bluesky if you’ve got suggestions you’d like to share. I also accept words of encouragement and compliments. :) The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is a powerful machine. Let’s see if we can find its limits. Stay tuned.

articles.title: Andrzej Sapkowski Talks New Witcher Books, Future Adaptations, and More
articles.summary: We interviewed The Witcher author Andrzej Sapkowski, who says the "sky is the limit" when discussing new novels following Geralt, more short stories, and potential future adaptations. His latest novel, Crossroads of Ravens, follows Geralt in his formative years and has recently been adapted into a full-cast audio drama.
articles.body:
The latest Witcher novel, Crossroads of Ravens, finally arrived in English last September, giving fans their first proper look at Geralt of Rivia's earliest days as a monster hunter.

I personally loved it, which probably won't come as much of a surprise given I've been eager to badger Andrzej Sapkowski with questions ever since I first picked up The Last Wish many moons ago.

I recently had the opportunity to chat with Sapkowski, the creator and author of The Witcher books , over email, alongside David French, the English translator of Crossroads of Ravens.

And, perhaps unsurprisingly, Sapkowski is every bit as sharp and disarmingly honest as you'd expect, with a wonderfully dry wit and a talent for delivering remarkably incisive answers. There's a scholarly flair to his responses, defined by a penchant for weaving classical Latin phrasing in wherever possible—a habit his English translator, David French, has also playfully dubbed "linguistic snobbery." Ha!

As a longtime fan, I'm delighted by the interview with both gentlemen, and I can't wait to share it.

We discussed (amongst plenty of other topics) the new Witcher prequel, Geralt's early years, the possibility of returning to that period of his life in future books , more short stories, and where Sapkowski sees the wider Witcher franchise going next. Whether that's a stage show like Game of Thrones , or another musical (yes, a musical, there have been two, I checked) , Sapkowski said he's nevertheless open to unorthodox suggestions.

An Interview with Andrzej Sapkowski, Author of The Witcher

In Crossroads of Ravens, we meet a younger, more inexperienced Geralt. What were the most rewarding and challenging parts of stepping back to write his early years?

Sapkowski: Well, it's not easy for an author nearly 80 years old to step into the shoes of an eighteen-year-old teenager. Fortunately, I still remember a thing or two from my youth. Including some experiences I shall never forget.

One of my favorite aspects of Crossroads of Ravens was seeing Geralt in rare moments of genuine panic, yet watching him make quick, split-second decisions and push through anyway. While I’m trying to avoid making a sweeping generalisation in questioning this—as Geralt certainly isn’t infallible in the main series—was it refreshing to write him in situations where he isn't yet fully used to what he’s dealing with? What was your thinking behind this?

Sapkowski: The narrative premise of my books makes Geralt a product of a targeted mutation making him a kind of superman. However, such a superman - always victorious, never defeated, omniscient and never doubting - seemed to me narratively uninteresting - if not outright boring. Therefore, despite all the infallibility resulting from his mutation, in the plot I gave Geralt some fallibilities, i.e. some imperfections. As well as susceptibility to err. Sometimes gravely.

What do you see as the biggest differences in mindset, morality, and temperament between the younger Geralt in Crossroads of Ravens and his older self in the main saga?

Sapkowski: That's rather obvious. Lack of experience and the harsh lessons from life associated with it. Development, mental and moral. Overcoming obstacles that accompany development. In other words, a classic rite of passage. A canonical trope for fantasy genre.

From your perspective, how does a full-length prequel novel demand an entirely different narrative engine and drive compared to something like the short stories from The Last Wish or the other Witcher novels?

Sapkowski: As Isaac Asimov once said: a short story is a straight line, while a novel is a plane. Point A to point B versus A times B squared. A comparison vivid enough to explain everything.

The relationship between Geralt and Preston was fascinating to read. What drew you to explore this specific dynamic, and how did you approach shaping a mentor relationship during Geralt's formative years? How does it differ from writing another mentor figure like Vesemir?

Sapkowski: Preston Holt is another classic and canonical trope for fantasy: the surrogate father figure, the archetypal mentor, a guiding teacher during Geralt's rite of passage. The genre features numerous such quasi-fathers and mentors in coming-of-age stories. Gandalf from LOTR, Dumbledore from the Harry Potter books, Allanon from the Shannara series, or Obi Wan Kenobi from Star Wars, to name just a few. But, as it turns out - and as storyline dictates - Holt is a rather deceitful mentor and I surely wouldn't put him in the same league as Gandalf. Or Vesemir.

Get 4 Months of Audible Standard for $0.99/mo

Did you draw on specific fables or myth tropes when constructing the encounters in Crossroads of Ravens, or has your relationship with fairytale/folklore exploration and subversion evolved since the early days?

Sapkowski: I evolve - or strive to evolve - on daily basis. Incessantly. And in every possible aspect. Or I wish it were like that. Either way, it amounts to the same thing. Wishes, contrary to popular belief, are horses. Sometimes.

I’ve always loved how your dialogue dances with an almost Shakespearean rhythm—characters politely trading sharp barbs, maneuvering around complex political situations while effortlessly delivering world-building. How do you go about constructing that rhythmic flow in your writing? Is it something that just comes naturally, or is it something that takes a lot more practice and effort to create?

Sapkowski: Both. Ease of writing is, as it seems to me, a feature of everyone who works with a pen, a condition sine qua non. If one doesn't have such ease, one doesn't become a writer. But ease alone is not enough. Without effort and painstaking work, one will not achieve good results.

Are there any monsters, characters, or concepts you’ve held onto over the years that you never found the right place for? What made them so tricky to fit in?

Sapkowski: First - at the beginning - is the idea and construction of the plot. The rest, including, quoting, "monsters, characters and/or concepts" results from the plot and serves the plot. Indeed, it happens that something from the mentioned suddenly begins to serve the storyline poorly or turns out as narratively damaging. Then it is thrown out of the plot and goes into the thesaurus. For possible use in the future.

Given your background before becoming a full-time author, was writing always the ultimate goal? What is your single best piece of advice for aspiring writers?

Sapkowski: My debut story entitled "The Witcher" was written when I was nearing 40, so it is rather difficult to describe my writing as my lifetime ultimate goal. I had many ultimate goals before I became a writer. Notwithstanding the fact that yes, now I think exactly so, I am now a full-time author and I intend to continue this state as long as possible. As for advice, I don't feel entitled to give it. I don't have the competence to advise.

Across your entire body of work, what type of scene remains the most challenging or demanding for you to write? Were there any scenes in Crossroads that you found particularly exciting/ challenging to tackle?

Sapkowski: Across my entire body of work? Every single one of them. Each was equally challenging as exciting.

Would you ever consider writing more short stories/ short story collections for The Witcher - similar to The Last Wish? Whether that’s focusing on Geralt or other characters within the series? (The Last Wish is still one of my all-time favorites and a real comfort read for me throughout my life).

Sapkowski: It is not an easy thing to create a good short story. This is much more difficult than writing a novel. Returning to Asimov's comparison: it is not easy to nicely and logically lead that straight line from point A to point B and that with a word count of less than some 8000 words. But if one succeeds, it is proof of writing mastery. May I remind just one example: Ernest Hemingway. Now, answering your question: yes, I am considering writing more short stories.

Do you feel there is room to explore Geralt’s early years further in future prequel books?

Having seen your characters expand into games, television, and comics, are there any unconventional formats or interactions you’d still like to see them explore? Stage plays, like Game of Thrones, for example?

Sapkowski: Does a musical count as a stage play? If so, there were already two. What else? I am open to suggestions. Even unconventional ones.

Why do you think Geralt resonates so deeply across medium boundaries—whether audiences are reading him on the page, watching him on screen, or playing as him in a video game?

Sapkowski: It is not my place to judge nor draw any conclusions here. Surely, one might suspect that both the books and the character somehow appeal to the reader worldwide - but perhaps that assumption is too presumptuous?

When writing Geralt’s dialogue, do you hear a specific mental voice for him? Does that inner voice differ between his younger and older self—and do famous screen/game audio performances ever cross your mind when writing?

Sapkowski: I definitely strive to ensure that the written text captures the specificity of how each individual character from the book speaks. That is, after all, the foundation and ABC of a writer's work. "Famous screen/game audio performances" have no influence on my writing in this aspect. Not even the slightest.

For any readers who have never read The Witcher before, how do you personally pitch or describe the essence of the series to them?

Sapkowski: I am not good at making essences. That's the specialty of marketing people, those who write blurbs on book covers. It's an art in itself. Many times I was asked to write such a blurb for somebody's book. I always refused. I couldn't.

Can you share any subtle hints or teases about what project you are working on next?

Sapkowski: I would prefer not to. Begging your pardon.

The Witcher 4 Unreal Engine 5 Tech Demo Screenshots

What books or authors have you most enjoyed recently, and do your current reading habits still bleed into your writing?

Sapkowski: I have recently enjoyed a lot of books, let me be allowed to mention a few, whereby the order is random:

Christopher Buehlman, Between Two Fires;

Did any of them - or any other, not listed - "bleed" into my writing? God forbid, no! And yes, confiteor, all of them. Somehow.

What books would you recommend to fans looking for inspiration or their next read? Perhaps anything similar to The Witcher, fantasy or otherwise?

Sapkowski: In addition to the titles just provided:

Grady Hendrix, Witchcraft for Wayward Girls;

V. E. Schwab, Bury Our Bones in the Midnight Soil;

Stephen Graham Jones, The Buffalo Hunter Hunter;

An Interview with David French, English Translator for Crossroads of Ravens

Sapkowski’s Polish mixes dancing prose, modern slang, and dry irony. What is your process for blending those elements into smooth, natural English?

I’m a big fan of Sapkowski’s writing and I love the elements you’ve mentioned above. A list of various other elements in his writing could, of course, be much longer than that. I wouldn’t say he uses that much modern slang. He certainly sometimes uses words which might jar with purists in the broadly medieval high-fantasy universe he navigates – I remember I wasn’t sure when he used the word ‘terrorism’ in dialogues between characters. I suppose the process you’re asking about is essentially the work of a literary translator. So you have to have an ear for those variations and do your best to transpose them into English – or whatever language it is you translate into. I guess my process is: thinking up possibilities, giving myself options, searching for synonyms, reading them aloud to myself, drafting, re-drafting and coming back to hear if they sound right.

Because Geralt is younger and less guarded in Crossroads of Ravens, did you adjust your choice of vocabulary or prose cadence to reflect his age?

Andrzej did. And I followed his lead. The sequence that springs to mind at once is when Holt tells Geralt off for using colloquial language. I played around with how slangy it should be and my line editor and I arrived at a consensus.

How do you preserve the sharp comic timing and dry wit of Polish dialogue when translating it for an English-speaking audience?

I give it my best shot and then the editor reads it. I’ve been known to ask if a gag struck home in English. There’s dry wit, but also vulgarity and slapstick at times. Andrzej’s humour isn’t one-note, there’s plenty of toilet humour in there too, along with more sophisticated sarcasm.

Were there any specific monster names, idioms, or turns of phrase in Crossroads of Ravens that gave you a real headache to translate into English?

Zatrawiec in Polish – which ended up as cynocephalus in English – was a bit of a headache.

The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past screenshots

What is one subtle quality of Sapkowski’s prose in Polish that you work hardest to protect across the language barrier?

My immediate thought was that in general terms Sapkowski’s work has to be a ripping yarn in English, just as it is in Polish. I want readers in English to keep turning those pages over and get the same emotional experience as Polish readers do.

But now that I think about it, I do my best to preserve Sapkowski’s linguistic snobbery, so I also try include words that some English readers might not have heard of – just as he does with obscure or archaic expressions most of my well-read Polish friends have no clue about.

How closely do you collaborate with Andrzej when working on a new translation, and do you ever consult him when a phrase doesn't easily translate?

We collaborate, in the sense that Andrzej now reads the entire manuscript after my work with the editor is complete. We started that with the Hussite Trilogy, which was full of real people from history and loads of geographical names, and we’ve continued it with Crossroads of the Ravens and the two new translations of The Last Wish and Blood of Elves. He’s a fluent and avid reader in several other languages than Polish and very thorough, so he offers various constructive suggestions. But it’s usually a handful or so. It’s happened in the past that I’ve asked him about something and he’s left the call up to me. I’ve also asked him to help me with the context and/or etymology and he’s replied to the effect that: ‘There isn’t any: I just made it up’.

Given how deeply ingrained iconic game performances (like Doug Cockle's Geralt) are for English-speaking fans, do those external adaptations ever influence how you rhythmically translate Geralt's speech, or do you strictly tune into Sapkowski's original Polish cadence/something else entirely?

There’s an infinite number of interpretations of any character in any literary work. It’s not the words on the page that change that, but the actor or reader speaking them. When I translate, it’s me and the words on the page. Nothing else is relevant.

There are occasions when Sapkowski might indicate if a person has a squeaky voice or a low growl and that gives readers a clue. I’m sure there’ve been studies about whether readers reading books actually generate sounds in their heads when they read or if it’s all done in silence. It’s totally different with games and audiobooks when we ‘find out’ how a character speaks. It’s also true we’ve all probably been disappointed at times to hear the way an actor has brought a character to life in a medium that involves sound when we’d imagined them totally differently. Or we’ve been delighted and couldn’t imagine anyone else voicing the character.

Sapkowski’s novels remain the bedrock of the series, but there's no denying that The Witcher has long since grown into something much bigger.

Alongside the games and their upcoming sequels and spin-offs , there’s now a Netflix adaptation , comics , a tabletop RPG , manga , and even a cookbook keeping the Continent alive in new and unexpected forms.

For help on where to start reading The Witcher, I'd recommend checking out our guide on the best order to read the incredible fantasy novels . And for more with the biggest fantasy authors, check out our big interview with Brandon Sanderson , where he discusses Game of Thrones , Wheel of Time , and the upcoming Mistborn movie .

Crossroads of Ravens by Andrzej Sapkowksi (translation by David French) is out in paperback now in the UK, and September 29, in the US.

articles.title: Next Witcher Novel Targeted for 2027 Completion, Author Andrzej Sapkowski Confirms
articles.summary: Author Andrzej Sapkowski confirms he is actively writing another new Witcher novel starring Geralt of Rivia, aiming to complete it in 2027.
articles.body:
The Witcher author and creator Andrzej Sapkowski has confirmed that he is already hard at work on Geralt's next adventure, and hinted to IGN that "the sky is the limit" for future prequels.

Sapkowski has confirmed that his next novel in The Witcher universe is already underway, with the Polish author targeting a 2027 completion date.

As reported by Redanian Intelligence , speaking on stage at the Copernicon convention in Torun, Poland, Sapkowski revealed that he has outlined his next book and is actively writing. While specific narrative details remain under wraps, Sapkowski shot down a fan question asking whether he would consider writing a novel centered on other characters, such as Yennefer of Vengerberg, confirming the story will once again focus on Geralt of Rivia.

The news aligns directly with comments Sapkowski made during our recent interview with the author and his English translator, David French . When asked whether he felt there was room to explore Geralt’s formative years further following the prequel Crossroads of Ravens, which tells us the story of an 18-year-old Geralt, Sapkowski offered a characteristically sharp response:

While Sapkowski is yet to confirm whether this next novel is unquestionably another Geralt prequel novel, it wouldn't be too much of a stretch to assume that's what we're likely getting.

Beyond this, Sapkowski also revealed to IGN that he is open to returning to the short story format that kicked off his Witcher novels with The Last Wish.

"It is not an easy thing to create a good short story," Sapkowski explained. "This is much more difficult than writing a novel... But if one succeeds, it is proof of writing mastery."

"It is not easy to nicely and logically lead that straight line from point A to point B and that with a word count of less than some 8,000 words... Now, answering your question: yes, I am considering writing more short stories."

Assuming Sapkowski hits his targeted completion date at the end of 2027, Polish readers can likely expect the book on shelves sometime in late 2027 or 2028, with English translations most likely following shortly after in late 2028 or 2029. If achieved, a four-year turnaround between Crossroads of Ravens and his next work would mark Sapkowski's fastest output since The Lady of the Lake in 1999.

Sapkowski has also said he is "open to suggestions" on any unconventional adaptations The Witcher could venture to next, amusingly pointing out that there have already been two musicals.

The Witcher certainly isn't slowing down either, in that regard, starting with a slate of full cast audiobook dramas that are set to release through the rest of 2026 and 2027. That starts with Crossroads of Ravens , the aforementioned Witcher prequel, and will be followed up by The Last Wish and Sword of Destiny in November.

Get 4 Months of Audible Standard for $0.99/mo

That's just the tip of the iceberg as well. In the world of video games, The Witcher 3: Remastered is soon to be released on September 29; including a slew of new features and performance updates .

There's also the surprise third Witcher 3 DLC expansion, called Songs of the Past , which will launch in 2027, alongside The Witcher 4, which is confirmed as a 2028 release , staring Ciri as the main protagonist. Season 5 of The Witcher Netflix series has reportedly delayed to 2027 , but still coming soon as well. Not a bad time to be a fan of The Witcher, to say the least.

articles.title: Fall 2007 Was the Greatest Stretch in Gaming – and Definitely Xbox – History
articles.summary: The fact that you can slice up the Fall of 2007 in so many different ways – best Xbox season ever, best PC season ever, best November ever – and the argument for its unmatched brilliance still holds up is iron-clad proof that it is, indisputably, the best season in video game history.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ryan McCaffrey, who worked at Official Xbox Magazine from 2002-2012 during the original Xbox and Xbox 360 era before joining IGN, where he remains “the Xbox guy.” In the run-up to Xbox’s 25th anniversary, he’ll be sharing his memories from the platform’s first quarter-century.

Sometimes, video game release schedules converge to create memorable superstorms that live on for years after the fact. The Fall of 1998 (Half-Life, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Doom 3, Metal Gear Solid, Grim Fandango) comes to mind, as does the Fall of 2004 (Half-Life 2, Halo 2, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, World of Warcraft). But for my money, the greatest season in gaming history was the Fall of 2007. It was so unbelievably brilliant that you could take just the Xbox 360 releases from this window and it still probably takes the cake. But when you add in PC, PlayStation 3, and Nintendo Wii releases, it’s an absolute murderer’s row of video games that will probably never be topped in a 3-4 month period.

At Official Xbox Magazine, we knew it was going to be big. But looking back and remembering our Game of the Year debate a few weeks after the dust settled (Rock Band won, and no I have no regrets about that), I’m not sure we were able to fully appreciate the gravity (gun) of the moment. One first-ballot Hall-of-Famer shipped after another. Take a look:

BioShock (August 21) : If you tried to argue that August 21 is still the Summer…I’d say I respect your point of view, but lots of kids are already back in school by August 21, so it counts as the Fall! Anyway, the original BioShock is an often-imitated, never-duplicated narrative-driven first-person shooter classic whose stunning underwater setting in the failed utopian city of Rapture – with its terrifying Big Daddies and mysterious Little Sisters – took gamers on a ride fit for a great novel,complete with a huge, jaw-dropping plot twist. Its only blemish is its weak final boss fight, but I’ve never seen anyone try to argue for that being enough to disqualify BioShock from the list of all-time greats. Emergent gameplay possibilities abounded, with Plasmids that let you ignite the pools of oil beneath an enemy’s feet on fire or to electrocute bad guys standing in puddles of water. This is legendary game designer Ken Levine’s magnum opus.

Halo 3 (September 25) : It’s wild to think about now, but for as successful as the Xbox 360 was, it didn’t launch with a big new Halo game. Instead, Halo 2 was a late release on the original Xbox, and thanks to Halo: Combat Evolved and Halo 2 having their backwards compatibility baked into every Xbox 360, gamers were able to continue right on playing the first sequel. But when Master Chief’s first next-gen adventure finally dropped and it was time to “finish the fight” that Halo 2 had left painfully unresolved , it was hugely anticipated and it actually delivered. The Chief got a proper sendoff in the final cutscene, making it one of the few sagas that actually stuck the landing.

The Orange Box (October 10) : Sometimes, Valve just does things , kinda like The Joker . The Orange Box was a ridiculous package of 10 out of 10 video games that any publicly traded game publisher would’ve split up and sold as a bunch of separately-sold 10 out of 10 video games. But not Valve. Steam makes Gabe Newell more money than he could ever know what to do with, so Valve, seemingly just for the love of the game, bundled Half-Life 2, Episode 1, and the then-new Episode 2, Portal, and Team Fortress 2 into a single $60 package. We’ll probably never see anything like this ever again…unless Valve drops Half-Life 3 out of nowhere in a “Crowbar Crate” with Portal 3 and Left 4 Dead 3. Which, honestly, we can’t 100% rule out.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare (November 5) : Infinity Ward’s third Call of Duty (Treyarch handled Call of Duty 3) not only brought the series out of World War II for the first time and into the modern era, but it also catapulted the franchise from Very Big Deal to The Biggest Deal, putting it in the same rarified air as Mario, Zelda, Halo (at the time), and Grand Theft Auto. It boasts an incredible campaign and multiplayer on which the entire last 20 years of Call of Duty have been built.

Assassin’s Creed (November 13) : You know it’s a killer list when this is the “worst” game on it. No one really spends time wistfully recalling the original. It was a heck of a four-hour gameplay loop that was more or less just repeated a couple of times, and most agree that Assassin’s Creed 2 – the start of the Ezio Trilogy – is where the series really took off. And more often than not, it’s a terrible idea to launch a new IP in the holiday season against established tentpole franchise sequels. That Ubisoft not only shipped Assassin’s Creed into the hurricane-force headwinds of Fall 2007 but the series gained a foothold and rose to become a megafranchise of its own speaks to how good the core idea of this “social stealth” game was.

Mass Effect (November 20) : I’ve already shared my extensive memories of this one elsewhere in this Xbox 25th anniversary retrospective series. But everything I said about Assassin’s Creed above also applies here. Maybe the lesson here is that publishers should place more big bets on bold new ideas…

Rock Band (November 20) : I’ve covered this one at length as well. You want to talk about a game that has aged beautifully? Rock Band is in fine-wine territory. The only hassle is finding functioning instruments to still play it with. It’s not a software problem, it’s an equipment problem. Even typing this makes me want to go play Rock Band immediately.

But even though the OXM offices had Xbox 360s on every desk, the staff were gamers who played every platform. So now let’s add in a PC exclusive, a PlayStation exclusive, and a Wii exclusive to really cement Fall 2007’s GOAT status:

Super Mario Galaxy (November 12) : My personal favorite 3D Mario game was also a bold reinvention of the 3D platformer from the masters of the genre. At this point, there isn’t a superlative that hasn’t been written about Super Mario Galaxy. Heck, it was so monumental that Nintendo and Illumination based the Super Mario Bros. Movie sequel around it earlier this year, almost 20 years after Galaxy debuted on the Wii.

Crysis (November 13) : Let’s just say there’s a reason that “Can it run Crysis?” became a meme. This wasn’t just a technical showpiece for the ages. It was also a tremendously good first-person shooter from the team that originally created Far Cry before Ubisoft bought it and took it over.

Uncharted: Drake’s Fortune (November 19) : The first Uncharted not only launched Naughty Dog into the upper echelon of game developers in the world and eventually paved the way for a movie starring Spider-Man , it took the mantle of third-person action-adventure gold standard from Tomb Raider, the series that arguably invented the genre. You could also make the case that this was the beginning of PlayStation’s insane run of top-shelf first-party exclusives that helped propel the PS4 to nearly the same record heights as the PS2.

The fact that you can slice up the Fall of 2007 in so many different ways – best Xbox season ever, best PC season ever, best November ever – and the argument for its unmatched brilliance still holds up is iron-clad proof that it is, indisputably, the best season in video game history.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: PlayStation Reveals New Limited-Edition Controller and Merch Collection With K-Pop Star Lisa
articles.summary: PlayStation has revealed a new collaboration with the K-pop star Lisa that includes a limited edition DualSense controller.
articles.body:
PlayStation has announced a new collaboration with the rapper, singer, and actress Lisa.

The collaboration will include a limited edition DualSense controller with an MSRP of $84.99 alongside a spread of additional merch that will be released in “two unique assortments.” The collection will go up for preorder in the U.S. on October 2 ahead of its full launch on October 30. The reveal also includes a new promotional video featuring, as you’d expect, Lisa herself.

The limited-edition controller has a relatively simple design with a soft grey color scheme. The main graphic is an artistic rendition of Lisa’s mascara-clad eyes, colored blue, with the iconic quartet of PlayStation buttons looped into her makeup look. The controller also features an "LL" logo on one side and Lisa’s signature on the back.

Additional items in the collection will include totes, sweaters, hats, and even stickers, making up a merch drop that extends beyond the usual PlayStation release and aligns a little bit more with what you’d expect from the K-pop star.

While the DualSense will initially only be available to preorder directly through PlayStation, additional items will be available through Lisa’s Amazon storefront .

No gaming company has been shy about collaborations, and limited-edition controllers have been a particular hit for both Xbox and PlayStation . Typically, though, these controllers are tied to a first-party game under either company’s banner, like PlayStation’s recent Wolverine line and Xbox’s Gears of War: E-Day controller . Collaborations with specific celebrities are more rare, with previous examples being limited to a Lebron James controller released back in 2023.

The PlayStation collaboration’s release will coincide with the release of Lisa’s next EP, Press Play, on October 23. Lisa, who is from Thailand, first entered the spotlight as the main rapper of Blackpink, a four-piece girl group under YG Entertainment. She has since grown into her own solo career with full albums like Rockstar, as well as acting roles like in HBO’s White Lotus .

Lisa is also no stranger to gaming collaborations, having recently headlined an entire Fortnite Festival season . Speaking on the new PlayStation collab, the artist highlighted that “Gaming is something I do whenever I have time to relax,” expressing that this collection “gave me a new way to be creative and show a different side of myself.”

PlayStation, in the meantime, continues to catch heat for its decision to cut production of physical discs. The company also recently saw a major shake-up with Hideo Kojima's decision to move development of his next espionage game, Physint, to Xbox .

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: Suspiciously Crisp-Looking Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire Footage Sparks Fresh Nintendo Switch Port Speculation
articles.summary: Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire footage shared by the official Japanese Pokémon account has sparked fresh speculation of a new Nintendo Switch release.
articles.body:
Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire footage shared by the official Japanese Pokémon account has sparked fresh speculation that the titles will be re-released for Nintendo Switch.

The Game Boy Advance classics can be seen again in the following video shared to social media by The Pokémon Company. On the surface, it's a playful post celebrating one of the game's many NPCs: Mr. Briney, known in Japanese as Old Man Hagi.

But eagle-eyed fans believe there's something suspiciously crisp and colourful about the footage, like it's been sourced from a new version of the game — perhaps even one that's running on the Nintendo Switch? After all, the fans say, Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen received similarly improved presentation when they arrived on Switch last year.

While Nintendo has said nothing officially about the launch of Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire re-releases, new launches for the games on Switch are widely expected . Not only were references to the games spotted in datamines of FireRed and LeafGreen's code, but those games also sold incredibly, incredibly well — with four million copies shifted in six weeks .

While controversial online at the time of their announcement , FireRed and LeafGreen's eye-opening $20 price point (each) did nothing to stave off demand to buy the games again (despite other GBA games simply being offered as part of the Nintendo Switch Online subscription). And all of this with little effort to modernize the titles on Nintendo's part, other than the unlocking of certain event tickets and the addition of a swear filter.

こらこら！ まて まて ピーコちゃん！ #敬老の日 #ハギろうじん pic.twitter.com/NhTjkeklBV — 【公式】ポケモン情報局 (@poke_times) September 21, 2026

Is there still time to announce and launch Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire before this year's lucrative holiday season? Just about. With Nintendo Switch 2 titles Pokémon Winds and Waves still up to a year away, these games would certainly buff The Pokémon Company's profits further in the back half of 2026. And we're still due to hear when exactly in October that FireRed and LeafGreen will get Pokémon Home support . A Ruby and Sapphire release around the same time would make a lot of sense.

Originally launched in Japan back in 2002, Ruby and Sapphire were the main titles for the Pokémon franchise's third generation, to later be joined by Pokémon Emerald. Set in Hoenn, these games introduced fan favorite creatures such as Mudkip, Treecko and Torchic, Kyogre and Groudon. Would you pay $20 to play one of these again?

articles.title: The First LEGO Mario Minifigure Sets Are Up for Preorder
articles.summary: Preorders are live for four of the first-ever LEGO sets featuring minifigures of Mario and the Mushroom Kingdom gang.
articles.body:
LEGO is gearing up to release a number of Super Mario sets that are unlike all previous Mario sets. These upcoming sets are minifigure-scale and feature minifigures of Mario and the Mushroom Kingdom gang. They're set to release January 1, but a number of them have just gone up for preorder at Amazon and Target . Let’s take a look.

LEGO Super Mario: Fire Luigi vs. Koopa Troopa Battle

LEGO Super Mario: Yoshi at Mario's House

LEGO Super Mario: Bowser's Rumbling Race

LEGO Super Mario: Mario's Beach Adventures

LEGO Super Mario: Luigi & Bowser Jr.'s Race

LEGO Super Mario: Fire Mario & Bowser's Castle

Note that all links above to Amazon and Target will let you preorder the sets in question. All links to the LEGO Store are just listings; preorders have not yet gone live there. I’ll update this article if they do.

The new minifigures include Mario (plus beach and fire Mario), Luigi (plus fire Luigi), Toad, Yoshi, Princess Peach, and even a Koopa Troopa. The sets come with plenty of enemies and recognizable items, like Goombas, POW blocks, Question blocks, racing Karts, banana peels, green and red shells, and more.

As usual, the sets have special interactive features. For instance, the $9.99 Mario’s Pipe Jump set has a lever that, when Mario jumps on it, sends the Goomba flying. The Bowser’s Castle set has a working drawbridge, trapdoors, and a lava ball launcher.

Previous Mario LEGO sets have all come in one of two flavors. One was LEGO sets for adults that were aimed at the 18+ age demographic, mostly honing in on nostalgia for things like the Game Boy , the NES console or Super Mario World’s Mario-riding-Yoshi sprite . I love those sets and hope they keep on coming. The other type of Mario set were the ones aimed at kids, with play functionality built in. I didn’t love those sets nearly as much.

I haven't gotten a close-up look at them yet, but I think this new batch of Mario minifigure-based LEGO sets strikes the perfect balance. Adults can collect and display them if they want, or kids can build them and play with them. For more, check out every upcoming LEGO set that's been announced so far.

articles.title: Hideo Kojima Could Be the Catalyst for an Xbox Turnaround
articles.summary: To use a sports analogy, Hideo Kojima is like a superstar athlete whose previous team (PlayStation) dropped him for, reportedly, salary-cap reasons. Xbox was all too happy to sign him, and unsurprisingly, they trotted him out at the Tokyo Game Show as the new face of the franchise. As they should. If this really was a sports team, a giant banner featuring Kojima’s face would be hung up on the outside of the stadium, and his jersey would be sold at the team shop.
articles.body:
To use a sports analogy, Hideo Kojima is like a superstar athlete whose previous team (PlayStation) dropped him for, reportedly, salary-cap reasons . Xbox was all too happy to sign him , and unsurprisingly, they trotted him out at the Tokyo Game Show as the new face of the franchise. As they should. If this really was a sports team, a giant banner featuring Kojima’s face would be hung up on the outside of the stadium, and his jersey would be sold at the team shop.

Getting Kojima’s next two projects as Xbox exclusives, or at least what could be Xbox exclusives – Xbox hasn’t yet announced that, but given CEO Asha Sharma’s refocus on exclusives and the common-sense thought that Xbox probably didn’t just sign Physint to publish it on PlayStation 6 – gives the next-gen Project Helix two big-name exclusives before Microsoft’s next-gen console has even been formally revealed.

I say Project Helix – it seems sensible to bet that Kojima’s projects (and thus whatever bonus his work can provide the Xbox brand) won’t arrive on Xbox Series X. OD is coming out before Physint, which Kojima himself said in 2025 is 5-6 years away, and while I suspect that the Series X will be supported for a longer period thanks to the fact that console prices continue to head in the wrong direction, past generation cycles would suggest that Helix will likely arrive before OD and Physint. Thus, OD might help kick things off fairly early in Helix’s lifecycle.

Looking beyond that, though, Xbox seems to – dare I say it – be heading in the right direction. I know, I know: I’ve said that before and so I probably sound like the Xboy Who Cried Wolf at this point, but let’s take a look at the pieces that Sharma has put in place so far. If Xbox really is serious about keeping its games off of rival consoles, then gamers might have plenty of reasons to jump ship from PlayStation back to Xbox in the next generation, just as they did from PS2 to Xbox 360.

Kojima will bring the prestige, which is something that Xbox has very much lacked, and will go a long way towards luring fans who’ve been loyal to him on PlayStation – that’s almost certainly why Microsoft signed him even after dropping four studios and laying off thousands of people mere weeks ago. But the biggest weapon in Xbox’s next-gen arsenal is undoubtedly The Elder Scrolls 6. Sharma raved about a recent demo she saw, but then again what else would she say about her most valuable asset? Still, there’s no denying that the first Elder Scrolls game in nearly two decades by the time it finally comes out will be a juggernaut. If Sharma has the intestinal fortitude to keep it off of PlayStation platforms, then that’s a whole lot of people buying her new console. I think she should and I think she will take this approach; if you’re going to return to exclusives you have to go all-in, lest you get the confusing mess Xbox’s exclusivity policy has been over the past couple of years.

OK, so thus far we’ve got OD (aka PT’s spiritual successor), Physint (aka Metal Gear Solid’s spiritual successor) and The Elder Scrolls 6. What else? Well, there’s Obsidian’s new Fallout game that’s being led by Fallout: New Vegas director Josh Sawyer. It remains to be seen whether or not the Fallout TV show can keep its pop-culture momentum going long enough to still be relevant when that project is finally ready to ship, but a new Fallout game from the makers of New Vegas is going to be huge regardless. Keep in mind that, like The Elder Scrolls, fans have been waiting a long, long time – the last mainline, single-player Fallout game is already over a decade old. And if its successor is exclusive? That’s a big, big deal.

Meanwhile, Fable will ship in five months on both Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5, but if it lives up to developer Playground’s pedigree established by its masterpiece Forza Horizon games , then the sequel is almost guaranteed to be both fantastic and exclusive to Xbox. Not to mention that Fable 2 should get turned around a lot faster than it took to build this reboot, which had to start from scratch.

Finally, there’s Forza, Halo, and Gears of War. The latter looks set to reestablish itself with E-Day, a prequel that helps revive the powerhouse series by returning its focus to the characters that we all love. If the whole thing is as awesome as what I’ve played so far , it sets up The Coalition to create another exclusive Gears adventure, which would presumably land in the middle of the Helix generation. Forza Horizon doesn’t need any fixing; the bigger question is, does Xbox dare to pull it off of PlayStation next time around after Forza Horizon 5 sold millions of copies despite launching years later on Sony’s platform?

Halo, on the other hand, absolutely needs fixing. Its future seems wildly uncertain, with Halo Studios leadership turning over recently and pivoting everything to Unreal Engine on the tech side. Halo: Campaign Evolved was fine , but does the studio even know what the next mainline game is yet? Is it Halo 7/Infinite 2? Is it a reboot? It’s already been five years since the last mainline Halo game, and it seems like it’s going to be at least five more. So…yeah, we’ll have to check back on that one.

Still, if rising console prices don’t crash the entire industry , then Xbox is set up to really turn things around in the Helix generation. It won’t happen overnight, and I’m not suggesting that they’ll suddenly overtake PlayStation in consoles sold, but the pieces are there for an Xbox 360 Redux-like situation, and I think we’d all be thrilled if that actually came to pass.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: 'I'm Still Low-Key Angry': Marvel Agents of SHIELD Star Says 'Real Followers Will Understand' Her Frustration the Series Isn't MCU Canon
articles.summary: Marvel's Agents of SHIELD star Chloe Bennet has said she's "still low-key angry" that the series isn't considered fully part of MCU canon — though has said that she would leap back into her role if required.
articles.body:
Marvel's Agents of SHIELD star Chloe Bennet has said she's "still low-key angry" that the series isn't considered fully part of MCU canon — though has said that she would leap back into her role if required.

Bennet played Daisy Johnson/Skye/Quake through all seven seasons of the MCU-adjacent TV show, which aired on ABC from 2013 until 2020. The series began as a spinoff from The Avengers starring Clark Gregg's Agent Phil Coulson, though became detached from the wider events of Marvel's movies over time, with later years seeing it diverge rather dramatically.

The series' exact place in Marvel canon has been hotly debated, though notably it is not included in the Disney+ "MCU Complete Timeline" section featuring every single canon MCU movie, TV series and one-off special. That's despite other pre-existing TV series from Marvel's Netflix era now being retroactively added, making 2015's Daredevil canon, but Agents of SHIELD not.

Marvel's Agents of SHIELD: The Many Lives (and Deaths) of Phil Coulson

"I'm still low-key angry that they don't fully acknowledge this as canon — the real followers will understand that," Bennet said, in an interview with Elle . "We were the first MCU TV show, and we did 130-something hour-long episodes. We spent a lot of time in people's homes, and I spent a lot of my life playing this character and this young woman growing into her power. There's a lot of symbolism in that, especially looking back now."

Marvel had once discussed Agents of SHIELD as being closely connected to the movies, and afforded the series several early cameos to tease the link between it and the big screen. Samuel L. Jackson's Nick Fury cameoed in an early episode, while Hayley Atwell's Peggy Carter popped up a couple of times. But later seasons — in part to avoid clashing with Marvel's movie plans — ventured into more standalone territory, with alternate timelines, alternate versions of Clark Gregg and an incarnation of Ghost Rider that will almost certainly be ignored when the Ryan Gosling movie rumbles along. The show ultimately wound up without acknowledging the Snap/Blip either.

All of that said, Bennet insisted she would still "totally" accept an invitation to reprise her Agents of SHIELD role in future, should Marvel come calling. "I'm obsessed with Daisy. I feel like I am Daisy. I would be so protective of her," the actress concluded. "I would love to play her with the growth that I’ve had since I've had a break from the role."

Perhaps in next year's Avengers: Secret Wars? If not then, it's hard to imagine when the series might ever be referenced again.

articles.title: EA Sports FC 27 Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos, Features, Career, FUT and More
articles.summary: EA Sports FC 27 from EA Vancouver and EA Romania continues the effort to win over fans on a global stage.
articles.body:
EA Sports FC 27 from EA Vancouver and EA Romania continues the effort to win over fans on a global stage.

The fourth entry in the "FC" branding for the series formerly known as FIFA, FC 27 follows up on a 77 Metacritic average for last year's game, which was a single point higher than FC 25.

An international sensation regardless, FC 27 continues the trend last year of going all-in around player feedback items. That means hyper-specific gameplay updates and quality-of-life items for game modes on top of the usual upgrades there.

Like usual, the first pass is great. The listed updates, gameplay and otherwise, sound good. The exception might be the polarizing addition of a social hub mode, but we'll get there. And as always, it's how FC 27 gets supported past launch that will ultimately decide its fate and standing within the community.

One glance shows the difference when it comes to FC 27 compared to prior years.

Footballer fluidity is a big emphasis this year and it shows in the form of weightiness and fewer pre-canned animations. This is seen, among other places, in the ability for more agile ball handlers to dribble well while off-balance.

It's impressive in the way it mirrors real life for pick-up-and-play fun, but also in the way it creates skill gaps for the competitive scene. Taking advantage of curbed runs, control through contact and attacking intent feels more rewarding compared to time invested.

These efforts loop in more than the ball handler, too, as a new two-player header system means more wow-worthy aerial duels that reward timing and skill.

Similar feel for more dynamic corner kicks, which live up the experience and bring it closer to the real thing.

A big emphasis also goes to defense, with enhanced manual defending options and another pass for the very strong tactics system. Fine-tuning how clubs implement play styles and specific roles in specific formations, then being able to swap them on the fly during a match, is just fantastic.

Seriously, being able to sort specific commands for specific possessions or phases and assigning certain individuals to specific duties within one single formation is an embarrassment of riches in terms of refined control.

Will the majority of the playerbase interact with this on a deep level? Maybe not, but it's the sports game equivalent to those mind-bogglingly deep tuning systems found in the best simulation racers.

It's an emphatic overall result. There's plenty of pick-up-and-play fun here, but deep-dive stuff, too. Post-launch support for problematic areas will brighten the outlook, too.

No shock here, but this series continues to nearly pace the entire sports market in this department.

Players might nitpick a very specific footballer's look or kit designs, but there's something to be said for the sheer immersiveness of matches. The feeling of size and scope behind a big international match in a huge stadium with the realistic chants and crowd reactions is just great.

Tack on the usual stuff, like fresh broadcast camera angles, new mannerisms from participants on the pitch and the nice lighting and physics, too.

At this point, commentary is a little stale. Good and immersive for brand new players, but even every-other-year players might be able to predict some of the lines before they happen. Voice-acting elsewhere is a little stilted and stands out in a bad way.

It's a small, little thing on this front too, but The Grounds' unskippable cutscenes are a slog and throwback to some of the horrific "stories" in sports titles of long ago.

Even so, it's an overall good, mostly immersive impression here, with solid points for the user interface (UI), too, in an era where sports games are extremely hit-or-miss in that area.

A year ago, the player career, weekly stuff and even archetypes got an overhaul to nice effect.

This year, the manager career gets some serious love.

For example, the transfer market is more dynamic in the way negotiations can take multiple stages. It's a little subjective, but it feels like clubs behave more realistically, too. Career mode also goes deeper on scouting and development

Generally speaking, the whole thing feels more random, too. Unexpected events even away from the pitch make it feel less like a video game and more like, well, real life.

Sparking a little cherry on top here is the presence of dynamic ratings. The continued shuffling of ratings in response to what is actually happening in the career mode is a really big deal. Whether it's short-term injury stuff or long-term developments, the impact is noticeable and appreciated.

Shiny and new this year is The Grounds, a sort of social space like those highly polarizing (but monetarily successful) ones found in games like the NBA 2K series.

Smack in the middle of all these is the central hub, The Terrace, which includes social areas, Clubhouses, stores and more.

As expected and needed, The Grounds loop in teaming up with friends via Clubs, 5v5 Rush, minigames, challenges, 1v1 sessions and quite a bit more.

Overall, The Grounds is a solid success because it takes past strong streetball efforts like Volta Football and combines it with some of the better elements of the NBA 2K social-space stuff. It won't be for everyone, but it's a nice chill way to keep the experience fresh.

A year removed from really emphasizing the always-online nature of Ultimate Team (FUT), this year, much of the love here is in player expression. The FUT Gallery arrives and lets players display their items. The Gallery Hub is a showcase for collections, including rare variants.

On the gameplay and actual collecting side, Squad Building Challenges have had their scoring streamlined in a great way. And there's an uptick in PVE modes to help solo players earn their season points in a way that feels fairer.

Short end of the stick here goes to player career and Clubs. The former gets a boost from the dynamic ratings and the latter from The Grounds, but as a whole, these two feel like they were on the dartboard to get the least attention this time out, as is the case for annual sports titles.

Microtransactions and currencies to juggle remain an issue. At launch, we're looking at coins, points, season passes and now gallery tokens. It's a lot to digest, by design, and how their presence impacts progression across various modes will be something to watch.

As always, FC 27 is a feat in the options department when accounting for the usual stuff, plus some expanded gameplay sliders this year to give players even deeper control over their on-pitch experience.

A social hub coming to FC is going to end up as polarizing as it gets for all the same reasons it is in other sports games.

The verdict? Players don't have to engage with it if they don't want to, but it shouldn't hurt to have it as part of the package. Even sports games should continue to be encouraged to try new things.

Overall, FC 27 is an easy enough recommendation. The on-pitch upgrades feel great and the effort to appease the wants of a global fanbase can be felt. There's deep replayability in career modes, too.

Annually, now, FC has been a solid entry point for new and lapsed fans alike, and this year's game is no exception to the praiseworthy rule.

articles.summary: Just ahead of the return of Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man on Disney+, Marvel will launch a new prequel comic bridging the gap between seasons of the show.
articles.body:
Spider-Man fans have been impatiently waiting for the animated series Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man to make its return on Disney+. The wait finally ends early in 2027, but that's not all. Marvel Comics is also launching a new Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man prequel comic in December.

As with the previous series and the various X-Men '97 comics , Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man is designed to bridge the gap between Season 1 and 2 of the animated series, revolving around a new conspiracy within Oscorp that springs up after Norman Osborn's downfall in Season 1.

As with the first Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man comic, the new series is written by Christos Gage and drawn by Eric Gapstur. Here's the official summary for the series:

And Norman Osborn may be out of the spider business, but Harry doesn’t think things are over just yet. Something’s happening at Oscorp, and Spidey and his friends need to figure out what it is!

articles.title: Bungie Says More Destiny Is Coming, Months After Ending Support for Destiny 2
articles.summary: Bungie has said it is "absolutely not done with Destiny" just months after its controversial decision to end ongoing support for Destiny 2.
articles.body:
Bungie has said it is "absolutely not done with Destiny" just months after the controversial decision to end ongoing support for Destiny 2 .

The five-minute upload features Bungie studio head Poria Torkan and head of product, GM of Marathon Josh Deane. The two executives start their surprise talk with fans, promising that Sony has not completely abandoned the Destiny brand after months of fans pleading to see them either return to Destiny 2 or eventually create Destiny 3.

"We're not asking for your trust," Torkan said, acknowledging some of Bungie's recent struggles. "We know we have to earn it, and to do that, we need our games to deliver in ways that exceed your expectations of what you've come to love about the games that we make – and that starts with Destiny.

Today, we’re sharing more about the future of Bungie, including our plans for Destiny, Marathon, and how we’re changing the way we work. Read more on : pic.twitter.com/F5tcXF0TsN — Bungie (@Bungie) September 21, 2026

Today, we’re sharing more about the future of Bungie, including our plans for Destiny, Marathon, and how we’re changing the way we work. Read more on : pic.twitter.com/F5tcXF0TsN

"Bungie wouldn't be what it is today without it. It's the foundation upon which everything else rests, and we are absolutely not done with Destiny. We have more stories to tell, but we have to do it right and give our teams the time they need to do justice to this amazing universe."

Deane clarified that Bungie's goal is to "return Destiny to its original promise." That means going back to "awe-inspiring mystery, the sense of discovery, and the promise of a community of Guardians rallying together, raging against impossible odds."

It's been a painful few months for the players who stuck by Destiny and Destiny 2 before substantial support came to an end with the Monument of Triumph update in June. Unfortunately, restoring that community and rebuilding trust will take even more time.

"I wish we could just flip a freaking switch, but we're going to commit to unvaulting the Destiny 2 campaigns, the destinations, the raids that never should have been ripped away to begin with," Deane added. "They were an essential part of our journey together and definitely a place where we built memories with y'all."

Bungie shared additional details with a post on its website . In a segment titled "Destiny Is Foundational to Our Future," the team excplitly called attention to the players who rallied together to give Destiny another shot at life . Through all of the uncertainty, comments , and livestream chat takeovers , it seems those in charge heard fans loud and clear.

"Your voices mattered, and the way you showed up made a real impact," the message said. "You reminded everyone how much this world, its history, and its future still mean to you."

As teased in the video, the first step to a future with more Destiny stories means unvaulting experiences that were previously locked away. The studio acknowledged that the vaulting certain experiences "had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny," adding that "Destiny 2 is more than just the content itself."

You did not go gentle into that good night. — dmg04 (@A_dmg04) September 21, 2026

You did not go gentle into that good night.

"It is a place where players have built memories together, formed lasting friendships, and shared experiences that have stayed with them for years. We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history."

Bungie said it is just getting started on the work required to unvault campaigns, destinations, and raids. All of this content will be made available for "all Destiny 2 players," though the developers caution that "bringing back this content is not as simple as restoring old files."

Changes made post-Beyond Light will require the studio to update lighting, encounters, combatants, and more. It's work that will take time, but the fact the effort is being put in at all is something that will no doubt have fans waiting on the edges of their seats, no matter how long it takes.

"When we look to the future of Destiny all up this restoration is the first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve," the message continued. "We’ll have more details on our unvaulting efforts in the coming months, and we’re very excited to share more about our vision to celebrate Destiny’s legacy and build its future with you all as soon as we can."

So, what exactly does this mean? While fans may not want to get their hopes up that this video serves as confirmation of Destiny 3 quite yet, Deane did say the plan is to deliver "new Destiny stories and games" that players deserve. In other words, the promise of more Destiny, a day many thought may never come, is here.

Aside from the untimely demise of the now-revived Destiny 2, Bungie itself has undergone a wave of significant changes in recent months. In June, the company was confirmed to have been impacted by layoffs affecting almost 300 staff . A few weeks ago, the company confirmed plans to sublease parts of its Bellevue, Washington headquarters .

Will Destiny 2 relaunch with a new name? Will we ever get Destiny 3? Will Bungie get to breathe life into its reported Destiny Infinity idea ? Only time will tell, but one thing is certain: Marathon will not be replacing Destiny .

articles.title: Bungie Bosses Promise to ‘Evolve’ Marathon, Deny Game Will ‘Replace’ Destiny
articles.summary: Bungie Studio Head Poria Torkan and Josh Dean, Head of Product and GM of Marathon, revealed plans to “evolve” Marathon as Bungie continues to navigate big internal changes.
articles.body:
Bungie Studio Head Poria Torkan, alongside the Head of Product and GM of Marathon, Josh Dean, revealed plans to “evolve” Marathon as Bungie continues to navigate big internal changes.

In a September 21 video message to fans, Torkan and Dean addressed what’s next for Marathon , saying the game is an “important part” of shaping where Bungie goes next.

"It didn’t reach as many players as we’d hoped,” Torkan admitted. “But we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.”

“We’re gonna anchor on what makes Marathon special and evolve it beyond the genre constraints that we’ve placed on it. We’re going to expand Marathon into a deeper survival experience that gives players more ways to take on its dangerous alien world,” Dean continued.

He outlined the team's goal for Marathon by the end of year one, saying that Bungie hopes to "preserve what you already love, but find ways to provide players with more agency in how you play, whether in PvE or PvP."

This news follows Bungie's plans to delay Marathon's next big update from late September to December. In a blog post published at the same time as Torkan and Dean's video message, Bungie reiterated that it "still [has] a lot planned for [its] October Nightfall Refresh and Symbiosis update in December." It also promised that players will get more Marathon news "later this week" regarding their vision for the future of the game.

Today, we’re sharing more about the future of Bungie, including our plans for Destiny, Marathon, and how we’re changing the way we work. Read more on : pic.twitter.com/F5tcXF0TsN — Bungie (@Bungie) September 21, 2026

Today, we’re sharing more about the future of Bungie, including our plans for Destiny, Marathon, and how we’re changing the way we work. Read more on : pic.twitter.com/F5tcXF0TsN

Marathon had a rough start since its launch in March; while it received critical acclaim upon release, according to data from SteamsCharts , it currently boasts around 1,390 active players, with a peak of just 2,630 in the last 24 hours. This is merely a small slice of Destiny 2's comparatively massive playerbase, and it seems the team at Bungie has taken notice of this, given its renewed efforts to reshape the game.

Perhaps most importantly, the two also confirmed that no, Marathon is not replacing Destiny, which had its own exciting announcements from the duo in that same video. Players, rejoice; there are "more stories to tell" in the Destiny universe, and Bungie wants to return the series to "its original promise" of "awe-inspiring mystery, the sense of discovery, and the promise of a community of Guardians rallying together, raging against impossible odds."

This comes as welcome news for Destiny fans, as Bungie infamously shuttered future content updates for Destiny 2 in May. The announcement didn't go over well, leaving players equal parts confused and distraught — but it seems the developer has decided against abandoning the IP in the wake of this strong community response.

This double-whammy of exciting announcements comes after major shifts for Bungie over the last few months. PlayStation CEO Herman Hulst confirmed "significant" layoffs for the studio in June, which included "most of the Destiny team and some Marathon team members." The developer also revealed plans to sublease a significant portion of its massive campus in Bellevue, Washington earlier this month.

With its renewed focus on Destiny and a sharper look at the future of Marathon, Bungie appears to be entering a new, exciting era, and fans can't wait to see what it's cooking up next.

articles.title: Pokémon Card Scalpers Are Moaning That the 30th Anniversary Set Isn't Profitable Enough for Them, as Rare Cards Have Been Made Easier to Find
articles.summary: Pokémon scalpers are complaining that the franchise's new 30th Anniversary set has been too generous with its rare cards — leaving resellers unable to generate their usual profits.
articles.body:
Pokémon scalpers are complaining that the franchise's new 30th Anniversary set has been too generous with its rare cards — leaving resellers unable to generate their usual profits.

Last week saw the long-awaited 30th Anniversary Pokémon Trading Card game set go on sale, with the usual scramble for stock among scalpers looking to make a quick profit. We reported on long lines outside stores in the U.S., plus frustration over "ghost chairs" left outside for days . In the U.K., there were ructions after accusations that a minor celebrity had ignored purchase limits and skipped the queue to snaffle up supply.

But as the dust settled, collectors quickly found that the 30th Anniversary set's rare cards... actually weren't that rare. Indeed, it appears that The Pokémon Company has done its best to defeat the usual scalper market by making all of the set's main cards findable with relative ease.

The only cards now being resold in the low thousands of dollars are the three eye-wateringly colored Red, Green and Blue Mew cards, which do seem to have a low drop rate. Otherwise, resale prices dip to well under $250 for everything else . Most of the top 15 expensive cards have been judged as being worth around $100 or less — a far cry from the thousands of dollars seen in previous sets.

This is great news for most fans, who will be able to fill their binders with the majority of cards — rather than a good chunk being left well beyond reach. However, it's less great news for scalpers who invested thousands of dollars in buying up stock expecting to make a huge margin.

"2-3 years ago, quite literally on this subreddit, many people were anticipating the 30th anniversary as a bull catalyst for exit strategies for their investments," complained one collector on dedicated reddit /r/PokeInvesting . "The literal complete opposite happened."

"It'll crush even more when more and more people start dumping," wrote another collector. "It's gonna be a bloody mess."

Pokémon TCG: 30th Anniversary Celebration Collection First Look

Not everyone is upset, however. In another /r/PokeInvesting thread, one fan has suggested that the 30th Anniversary set's easy hit rates were good for money-making in the long-term. Why? Because more children and potential collectors will be lured in by the high rate of rare cards this time around — only for things to inevitably be reversed in future.

"I actually think this set is extremely healthy for the hobby long term," TommyC6852 wrote. "This is a set that is a blast to open; and should be decently available for the common collector. At some point you want people to have fun; and this set should give the hobby the breath of fresh air that it needs. The more fun people have, the longer they stay in. The longer people stay engaged; the higher our investments will go."

The next Pokémon trading card set, Mega Evolution — Delta Reign, will launch as soon as November.
